channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The US and Saudi Arabia announced a civilian nuclear deal that Trump tied to Riyadh recognising Israel, the EU cautiously welcomed a Gaza peace plan, and a Russia-sanctions bill faces a tough path in Congress amid wider doubts about US reliability.
item.description:
Saudi Arabia announced a deal letting US companies build civilian nuclear power plants in the kingdom — potentially including uranium enrichment — eight years after it warned it would pursue nuclear weapons if Iran did. Trump declared the deal "totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords" by recognising Israel, a condition experts warn sets a precedent others in the region could follow. Diplomacy moved on other fronts: EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas called a proposed Gaza peace plan a "constructive" step if fully implemented, while cautioning that verifying compliance will be hard; and Trump hosted Israel's Netanyahu and Ukraine's Zelensky at the White House. Meanwhile a Russia-sanctions bill — authorising up to 100% tariffs on the biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas, which would hit India and China — faces a tough road in Congress as lawmakers balk at the trade powers it hands the president. Commentators note a broader pattern: allies are recalibrating ties as they question US consistency, with some polls finding China now seen as the more predictable partner.

Industry Impact

The Saudi nuclear deal signals large long-run construction and industrial-materials opportunity in the Gulf if it proceeds, and reinforces the region's pivot from pure oil exporter to diversified industrial economy. For chemical trade, the Russia-sanctions bill is the item to watch: 100% tariffs on major Russian-energy buyers would disrupt India's and China's energy costs and could ripple into feedstock prices and trade flows. The wider realignment of alliances raises the premium on geographically diversified sales and sourcing, as political risk becomes less predictable.

The Independent | Asharq Al-Awsat | Arab News | The Times of India | The Economic Times

item.title: Global wheat output is forecast to fall 24 million tonnes next season on El Niño weather and war-driven costs, half of England is back in serious drought threatening housing plans, and low Rhine levels are again raising costs for German industry.
item.description:
Climate and weather stress compounded across regions. The International Grains Council projects global wheat production will drop about 24 million tonnes in 2026-27 as farmers in North America, the EU, the UK and Australia cut acreage or switch crops under El Niño risk and higher input costs tied to the Iran war, trimming world trade and stocks. In England, the Environment Agency declared half the country in serious drought for a second straight year, warning of consequences for the economy and environment — and noting that the water-stressed south and east are exactly where the government wants to build 1.5 million homes, putting the "build, baby, build" agenda at risk. In Germany, persistently low water on the Rhine (just 71 cm at Cologne, more than two metres below average) is forcing freighters to carry less and raising costs for industry and logistics; nuclear plants in Hungary, Romania and France have had to cut output because river water is too low or too warm. Localised flooding also hit Palghar in India and a hospital in Manitoba, Canada.

Industry Impact

Low-water events on the Rhine are a recurring, direct risk to European chemical logistics, since much feedstock and product moves by barge; shippers should expect surcharges and rerouting through the dry season. Drought and the wheat shortfall feed agricultural-input and food-price inflation, supporting demand for crop-protection and fertiliser chemistries while raising bio-based feedstock costs. Water stress constraining UK housing also tempers construction-chemicals demand there. These are becoming routine planning variables rather than one-off shocks.

The Hindu Business Line | The Guardian | Tagesschau | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | The Times of India

item.title: China now makes eight of every ten humanoid and quadruped robots sold worldwide, robot-maker Unitree flagged US-market risk as Washington bars new Chinese robots from import, and Xi Jinping urged wider military use of AI and autonomous systems.
item.description:
China's grip on advanced robotics came into sharp relief. The National Development and Reform Commission said 80% of the humanoid and quadruped robots sold globally are now made in China. The dominance is being tested by US policy: the Federal Communications Commission added foreign-made advanced robots and power inverters to its "Covered List," so new models cannot obtain the FCC certification needed to sell in the US — Unitree Robotics, filing for a STAR Market IPO, warned this could hit future models even though existing certified products can still be sold. Washington paired the robot import ban with sanctions on more than 80 Chinese research institutions. Domestically China is pressing ahead: a former northeastern industrial base (Heilongjiang) is reinventing itself around robotics, and Xi Jinping used a Politburo study session to call for more defence applications of AI and autonomous technologies as he pushes to modernise the armed forces. China's electronic-information manufacturing value-added rose 14.8% in the first half, and integrated-circuit exports jumped 88.7%.

Industry Impact

Industrial automation and robotics are a rising demand pool for ACS (assembly adhesives, potting compounds, protective coatings for sensors and actuators), and China's dominance shapes where that value is captured. US import restrictions may fragment the market into "Chinese" and "non-Chinese" robot supply chains, creating openings for Western and allied makers but also raising costs. For manufacturers, cheap and rapidly improving Chinese automation is a productivity opportunity; for Western robot and component makers it is a competitive threat mirroring the broader China-overcapacity theme (see other insight in this alert).

China Economic Net | China Daily | Bjd.com.cn | Commercial Times | Bloomberg | Xinhua

item.title: Indian car sales rose 34% in July, the central bank was set to hold rates, Modi and the new UK prime minister pledged to deepen ties under their trade deal, and Indian drugmakers resisted pressure to relocate to the US despite tariff threats.
item.description:
India offered a rare cluster of good news. July car sales jumped an estimated 34% to about 469,000 units, with Maruti, Hyundai and Mahindra raising capacity and Tata extending its EV lead; 125 basis points of first-half rate cuts have made home loans cheaper, though city prices are up sharply. The Reserve Bank of India was expected to hold its repo rate this week as it balances inflation and growth. Diplomatically, Prime Minister Modi and new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged to take their Comprehensive Strategic Partnership "to new heights" and maximise the recently operational India–UK trade deal (CETA). On tariffs, Indian pharmaceutical firms said they are in no rush to move to the US despite Trump's threat of up to 200% duties on generics after a transition period, preferring to lean on existing US plants and keep India as their production base. Industrial ambition is visible too: defence-goods output hit INR 1.7 trillion in FY26, and construction began on a semiconductor assembly-and-test (OSAT) facility in Andhra Pradesh.

Industry Impact

India is increasingly the counterweight to a soft European and slowing Chinese picture for chemical demand: strong autos, construction and electronics build-out support coatings, adhesives and sealants volumes, and the semiconductor and defence investments open new specialty-materials markets. The India–UK deal and India's reluctance to decouple from its home base reinforce it as a stable growth geography. Rising local commodity costs (steel, aluminium, copper, rubber) are the main margin watch-item for suppliers serving Indian manufacturers.

The Economic Times | The Hindu Business Line | New Indian Express | Business Standard | The Times of India | The Economic Times

item.title: Taiwan's economy grew almost 13% year-on-year in the second quarter — its best in decades — as AI-hardware demand lifted exports, prompting forecasters to raise 2026 estimates toward 11%, while Hong Kong and Singapore also pointed to AI-led strength.
item.description:
Taiwan's statistics bureau reported second-quarter GDP growth of 12.92% year-on-year, blowing past expectations, with exports up 21.6% and imports up 18.3% on surging demand for artificial-intelligence hardware. The Taiwan Institute of Economic Research lifted its 2026 growth forecast to 10.38%, and foreign banks followed — UBS and ING raised theirs to around 11%. The AI tailwind is regional: Hong Kong said it will raise its annual GDP forecast after 5.1% first-half growth, with the financial secretary citing strong global demand for AI products; and Singapore's manufacturers, surveyed by the Economic Development Board, stayed net-optimistic about the second half on AI demand, though less exuberantly than a quarter earlier. The standout risk inside Taiwan's boom is domestic property: unsold presale and second-hand housing inventory hit a record even as transaction volumes halved, a growing imbalance beneath the export-led headline.

Industry Impact

The AI-hardware cycle is the single strongest demand driver in Asia right now, and it pulls through directly to electronics-grade ACS materials — semiconductor packaging, thermal-interface and encapsulation chemistries — where Taiwan, Korea and their suppliers dominate. Producers exposed to this cluster benefit, but the concentration also amplifies the supply-shock risk highlighted by Japan's quake and the memory crunch (see other insight in this alert). Taiwan's property overhang is worth monitoring as a potential drag on construction-chemicals demand there.

Asharq Al-Awsat | Commercial Times | Commercial Times | South China Morning Post | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: Eurozone inflation edged up to 2.9% in July, cementing expectations of a September ECB hike, while the Bank of England held rates in a dovish-leaning 6-3 vote and the Bank of Japan signalled it may speed up hikes after a currency intervention.
item.description:
The war's energy shock is pulling major central banks in different directions. Euro-area inflation rose to 2.9% in July from 2.8%, driven by higher oil prices after the US–Iran ceasefire collapsed; economists and investors now widely expect the European Central Bank to raise rates again in September, following its June hike. In the UK, the Bank of England held rates but the 6-3 split — with Catherine Mann joining the hawks pushing for an immediate hike to offset the energy shock — actually masked a dovish shift among the deputies, who grew more relaxed about second-round inflation. The Bank of Japan held at 1% but Governor Ueda warned it may accelerate hikes to avoid "falling behind the curve," after the yen hit a 40-year low and the government intervened to prop it up. India's Reserve Bank was expected to hold its repo rate this week, balancing inflation risks against growth. The common thread is an energy-driven inflation impulse that keeps the hawks engaged even as growth softens.

Industry Impact

Persistently higher policy rates raise the cost of capital for chemical producers' capacity expansion and decarbonisation projects, and a firmer ECB path keeps European financing conditions tight just as industry is already squeezed. Currency swings matter for input costs and competitiveness: a stronger yen raises costs for Japanese producers, while any euro moves around the ECB decision affect the price of dollar-denominated feedstocks. Treasurers should plan for at least one more ECB hike and continued FX volatility into the autumn.

Lianhe Zaobao | Financial Post | The Financial Times | The Hindu Business Line | Die Zeit

item.title: China's State Council promised concrete measures to lift domestic demand and the central bank pledged loose policy and ample liquidity, as Beijing drafts a 2026–30 demand-expansion plan backed by CNY 800 billion of new policy financing.
item.description:
With factory activity slipping into contraction, Beijing shifted from signalling to specifics. A State Council executive meeting chaired by Premier Li Qiang on 31 July called for "more concrete measures" to sustain high-quality growth and ensure a strong start to the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–30), stressing effective use of existing policy plus timely new "incremental" measures and a stronger push on domestic demand. The People's Bank of China, at a mid-year working meeting and in follow-up statements, pledged to keep liquidity ample and maintain an "appropriately loose" monetary policy, to match credit and social financing to growth targets, to facilitate panda-bond issuance and support local-government debt resolution. Separately, the National Development and Reform Commission said it is drafting a dedicated five-year plan to expand domestic demand for 2026–30 and will accelerate CNY 800 billion of special-purpose bonds and new policy-based financial instruments during the third-quarter construction peak, funding "six networks" of logistics, pipelines, communications, computing, power and water infrastructure.

Industry Impact

Chinese stimulus is a swing factor for global chemical demand: infrastructure and construction spending drives volumes for coatings, sealants, adhesives and construction chemicals, and looser credit supports the property and auto sectors that consume them. A credible domestic-demand push would help absorb some Chinese overcapacity at home rather than exporting it — modestly easing the very "China Shock 2.0" pressure on European producers (see other insight in this alert). Watch whether the CNY 800 billion actually deploys in Q3, since past stimulus pledges have sometimes underwhelmed on execution.

Xinhua | China Daily | The Straits Times | Kompas.com | China Economic Net

item.title: With US tariffs on China cut, producing in Vietnam and Thailand is no longer cheaper, prompting some US firms to consider moving output back to China, as Washington presses Beijing on farm and rare-earth pledges before a September Xi–Trump summit.
item.description:
A notable reversal is under way. After the Trump administration raised China tariffs to 145% in 2025, many US companies shifted production to lower-cost Southeast Asian countries such as Thailand and Vietnam. But Washington has since cut China tariffs sharply — its new Section 301 "forced-labour" duties put China, Vietnam and others at a similar 12.5% — so the Southeast Asian cost advantage has eroded and some firms are now considering returning to China's larger, more efficient supply base. On the diplomatic track, US Trade Representative Greer, Treasury Secretary Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held a call to prepare a September visit by Xi Jinping to the US; Bessent said the US expects Beijing to fully honour commitments on US farm purchases and rare earths, and Senator Steve Daines is expected back in Beijing to finalise the summit agenda, which includes an AI cooperation track. Beijing, for its part, lodged "serious concern" over US trade barriers.

Industry Impact

For globally sourced ACS and specialty-chemical supply chains, the reshoring reversal matters: the "China+1" diversification of 2024–25 may partly unwind where China offers scale and cost that Southeast Asia cannot match, though political risk keeps dual-sourcing prudent. A successful September summit that locks in rare-earth and agricultural commitments would ease two of the industry's biggest input-security worries — rare earths for electronics and catalysts, and stable agricultural feedstocks — while any breakdown would revive tariff and export-control volatility.

Lianhe Zaobao | MarketScreener | Commercial Times | Commercial Times | Handelsblatt

item.title: Cost-cutting at BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen is starving German auto suppliers of bank credit, China's car-industry profits fell nearly 20% in the first half, and Indian car sales jumped 34% — a widening gap between struggling and booming markets.
item.description:
The cost-cutting drives at BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen are having expensive knock-on effects for German automotive suppliers, according to WirtschaftsWoche: with market prospects gloomy, suppliers increasingly struggle to secure the bank loans they need to fund the shift to electric and software-defined vehicles, and credit insurer Atradius warns the manufacturers' austerity programmes are intensifying the squeeze. The weakness is visible in the numbers elsewhere too: China's automotive-manufacturing sector posted a 19.5% drop in first-half profit to CNY 195.4 billion even as revenue edged up 1.8%, leaving margins at just 3.8%. Against that, India is a standout — July car sales rose an estimated 34% to about 469,000 units, with Maruti, Hyundai and Mahindra absorbing higher steel, aluminium, copper and rubber costs while raising capacity, and Tata extending its lead in electric passenger vehicles. Chinese and German carmakers also met in Beijing to align smart-connected-vehicle standards, a rare note of cooperation amid trade friction.

Industry Impact

Automotive is a core ACS end-market (structural adhesives, sealants, coatings, battery-assembly materials), so supplier distress in Germany is a direct concern: financially stressed Tier-1s and Tier-2s delay programmes, squeeze their own suppliers on price, and defer investment in new bonding and lightweighting technologies. The contrast with India's boom argues for weighting growth toward Asian OEM platforms while managing credit and payment risk across the European supplier base. Thin Chinese margins also signal continued price aggression from Chinese EV makers expanding abroad.

WirtschaftsWoche | China Daily | The Economic Times | The Hindu Business Line | South China Morning Post | MarketScreener

item.title: A magnitude-7 earthquake in Japan's Kyushu chip-and-auto heartland forced Toyota, Renesas and Sony to halt output just as an AI-driven memory shortage tightened supply, and Apple fell nearly 10% on component constraints.
item.description:
The 28 July earthquake near Kumamoto struck a region so dense with semiconductor plants it is called Japan's "Silicon Valley," and it killed at least 34 people. Toyota suspended three Fukuoka plants and idled one in Aichi; Honda, chipmaker Renesas and Sony also cut or halted production, and Toyota supplier Aisin stopped an engine-and-door-parts plant in Kumamoto. The disruption lands at the worst moment: an AI-driven data-centre boom — nicknamed "RAMageddon" — is straining global supply of advanced chips and memory. Apple's shares fell nearly 10% after it guided to 9–11% revenue growth, below the ~12% expected, warning it cannot fully meet iPhone and Mac demand because chip and memory capacity is fully booked; the slide threatened to cede its "most valuable company" crown to Nvidia. The strain is spreading: India reports a printed-circuit-board shortage driven both by the AI diversion of components and by Iran's strikes disrupting PCB chemicals. Verisk estimates insured property losses from the quake at JPY 220–340 billion, before payouts under Japan's earthquake-insurance scheme.

Industry Impact

Electronics is a growth market for ACS (chip-packaging adhesives, thermal materials, conformal coatings), so both the quake and the memory crunch matter directly. Near term, plant shutdowns and allocation of scarce chips/memory to AI hardware mean longer lead times and higher prices for electronics-linked materials and for the automakers that consume them. The episode is a reminder that a single seismic event in a concentrated cluster can ripple through autos, semiconductors and the specialty chemicals feeding both — an argument for supplier diversification and buffer stock on critical electronic-materials inputs.

South China Morning Post | Commercial Times | The Independent | WirtschaftsWoche | The Economic Times | MarketScreener

item.title: China's new five-year plan targets a CNY 8 trillion recycling industry by 2030, the EU debates whether its Circular Economy Act can scale material recovery, and New York Democrats are split over whether chemical recycling counts as "recycling".
item.description:
Recycling and circular-economy regulation moved to the front of the ACS agenda this run. China's National Development and Reform Commission issued its 15th Five-Year Plan for the circular economy, aiming to lift the resource-recycling sector's output to CNY 8 trillion by 2030 and raise resource productivity about 16% from 2025, with a dedicated push to recover the coming wave of retired power batteries, solar panels and wind turbines (its "new three"). In Europe, campaigners argue the forthcoming Circular Economy Act must actually fix the fact that end-of-life cars, batteries and scrap are being exported out of the EU, starving domestic battery and aluminium recyclers of feedstock. In the US, New York's Packaging Reduction and Recycling Infrastructure Act would cut single-use plastics, shift waste costs onto producers, and ban additives such as phthalates, bisphenols and PFAS — but it splits lawmakers by excluding chemical recycling from the definition of "recycling", which industry opposes. Two market signals rounded out the picture: phenolic resin for tyres and rubber is forecast to grow about 7% a year to 2033, and ADM is investing over USD 16 million to expand natural-colour production in Kentucky.

Industry Impact

These rules directly reshape ACS demand and compliance. Bans on specific additives and tighter packaging rules affect which chemistries can be sold and force reformulation; the treatment of chemical (advanced) recycling determines whether producers can count it toward recycled-content targets — a live commercial question for adhesives and coatings tied to packaging. China's scale-up of battery, solar and wind recycling both creates raw-material streams and intensifies competition in recovered materials. Producers should track feedstock-availability rules in the EU act closely, since recyclate access is becoming a competitive input.

China Economic Net | China Economic Net | Transport & Environment | Politico | Rubber World | MarketScreener

item.title: Germany's industry body warned of a "China Shock 2.0" hitting the whole of industry, France and Germany called for an EU roadmap to defend European producers, and the bloc's trade deficit with China now runs above EUR 1 billion a day.
item.description:
Tanja Gönner, head of the Federation of German Industries (BDI), warned that Germany faces a "China Shock 2.0" — but where the first shock after China's 2001 WTO entry hit specific sectors with cheap goods, this one hits industry as a whole through dependence on Chinese critical raw materials, a significantly undervalued yuan, and state-driven overcapacity flooding the EU single market as China's weak domestic demand and US market barriers redirect exports. China is also openly targeting leadership in key technologies. France and Germany, at their mid-July ministerial council, jointly branded China as "challenging our economy" and called for an EU roadmap of trade-defence instruments; EU leaders have already mandated the European Commission to build additional tools against subsidised imports. Commentators note the bind: the EU's trade deficit with China exceeds EUR 1 billion a day, yet the bloc's 27 members have very different exposures to China, undermining a united front. Germany's own signals stayed mixed — Q2 output beat expectations, but July unemployment rose unexpectedly to 6.4%, passing three million jobless for the first time in years.

Industry Impact

This is the strategic backdrop for every European chemical and manufacturing producer: a stagnant home market, rising Chinese competition in mid- and high-value goods, and mounting political pressure for tariffs and trade defence. For ACS and specialty-chemical makers it cuts both ways — potential protection from subsidised Chinese imports, but also the risk of retaliation and higher input costs if the EU raises barriers on Chinese raw materials the industry depends on. Expect trade-defence cases and "de-risking" rules to become a bigger planning variable through 2026.

Handelsblatt | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | Human Rights Watch | Les Echos | The Standard | Hürriyet Daily News

item.title: The US and Israel are weighing a land blockade to seal Iran's seven borders while Gulf states press China to reopen the Strait of Hormuz; oil ended July about 20% higher, and the disruption is now lifting prices on paint, packaging and food.
item.description:
After months of air strikes failed to force Tehran to yield, Washington and Israel are discussing a land blockade — pressing Iran's seven neighbours (Iraq, Turkey, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Armenia and Azerbaijan) to tighten or close border crossings and choke trade. That would be a sharp escalation on top of the naval fight around the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow sea lane that normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil. Gulf Arab states, whose own energy exports are being throttled, are testing China's influence: Beijing is both a major Gulf oil buyer and Iran's biggest trade partner, and Foreign Minister Wang Yi has held dozens of calls seeking a fresh ceasefire. Crude ended July up roughly 20%, though it swung violently and fell early this week after Trump said Iran and several Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to finalise a deal to reopen Hormuz. With traffic collapsing through Hormuz and the Houthi-blockaded Bab al-Mandab, tanker freight rates have multiplied and a "dark fleet" is rerouting cargoes the long way around.

Industry Impact

For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) industry the pass-through is now concrete, not theoretical. The Wall Street Journal reports companies raising prices on oil-linked goods — Sherwin-Williams plans an 8% paint-price increase from 1 September — because crude, solvents and packaging inputs are dearer and Gulf shipping is longer and pricier. India's electronics makers already face a shortage of PCB chemicals traced to Iran's strikes on Saudi facilities. Chemical and coatings buyers should plan for higher naphtha and additive costs, freight and insurance surcharges on Asia–Europe lanes, and continued volatility until a Hormuz reopening is actually confirmed.

The Times of India | The Economic Times | The Economic Times | Yahoo Finance | Handelsblatt | Lianhe Zaobao
